references.label: AA LAST 2024
references.citation: Royal College of Anaesthetists & Association of Anaesthetists. Management of severe local anaesthetic toxicity: a joint guideline. 2024.
references.excerpt: Stop injecting local anaesthetic, call for help, maintain the airway with 100% oxygen and control seizures with a benzodiazepine; propofol is not recommended when there is any cardiovascular instability. Give intravenous lipid emulsion 20%: an initial bolus of 1.5 ml/kg over 1 min followed by an infusion of 15 ml/kg/h, with up to two further boluses and doubling of the infusion rate if cardiovascular stability is not restored; do not exceed a total of approximately 12 ml/kg (about 1000 ml in a 70 kg adult). Continue cardiopulmonary resuscitation for a prolonged period and transfer to critical care.

references.excerpt: AAGBI guidelines on the management of LAST were first published in 2007 and updated in 2010. Since then, further research and case reports have been published that have prompted this update. The format follows that of the previous versions, with a checklist and a treatment algorithm. The working group also reviewed the role of lipid emulsion in the resuscitation of children, which is now included in the main guideline.

references.excerpt: Reduce individual epinephrine boluses to less than 1 mcg/kg, avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, beta blockers and further local anaesthetic, and give lipid emulsion 20% by bolus and infusion; the total lipid emulsion dose should be limited to approximately 12 ml/kg.

cards.question: How should local-anaesthetic dose limits be selected?
cards.answer: Use the exact product, route and procedure table, not a universal maximum-safe dose. Named UK lidocaine 2% (emc 15150) limits a single dose to 4.5 mg/kg and 300 mg; more conservative local policies may apply. Xylocaine with adrenaline (emc 2397) has an adult single-dose ceiling 500 mg. Named bupivacaine field-block/infiltration (emc 11611) limits 150 mg; levobupivacaine (emc 13644) has single-dose 150 mg and daily 400 mg limits. These scopes are not interchangeable with spinal, major nerve blocks or IVRA; no universal ropivacaine/prilocaine maximum is inferred. Prior doses, mixed agents, vascularity, body-weight basis and patient factors matter. Below a listed ceiling, toxicity remains possible.

cards.question: How does pKa of a local anaesthetic relate to onset of action?
cards.answer: Only the unionised form crosses the nerve membrane. The closer the pKa to physiological pH, the higher the proportion unionised, and the faster the onset. Lidocaine pKa 7.9 — ~25 % unionised → onset 2–5 min. Bupivacaine pKa 8.1 — ~15 % unionised → onset 10–15 min. In infected tissue (low pH), more drug is ionised → poor onset (textbook reason to avoid LA in abscesses). Chloroprocaine (pKa 8.7) is exception — fastest onset due to high concentration used.

cards.question: Outline the management of local-anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST).
cards.answer: RCoA/Association of Anaesthetists 2024 algorithm: STOP injection, call for help, ABC (100 % O₂, secure airway, IV access). Manage seizures (small dose benzodiazepine or propofol). Treat arrhythmias (avoid lidocaine, calcium, vasopressin; use small adrenaline 1 µg/kg). Give 20 % Intralipid: 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 15 mL/kg/h infusion, repeat bolus up to 3×, max 12 mL/kg total. Continue CPR — long resuscitation often successful. Refer to ITU and report to NPSA / Lipid Rescue registry.
